cases.description: empty input is returned unchanged
whitespace-only input short-circuits
with enabled=false the filter is a no-op, even on obvious fillers
Rule A: a leading filler is removed
cases.input: um the meeting is at noon

cases.description: Rule A: several fillers in one burst
cases.input: um so like the meeting is uh at noon
cases.expected: so the meeting is at noon

cases.description: Rule A: multi-word fillers ('you know')
cases.input: the meeting you know is at noon

cases.description: Option 2 for #117: utterance-initial capitalised fillers are stripped — Whisper capitalises the first word, so 'Um' at position 0 is almost always a filler, not a proper noun
cases.input: Um the meeting is at noon

cases.description: utterance-initial 'Uh' is unambiguous and still stripped

an AMBIGUOUS multi-word filler is not relaxed at position 0: 'You know the meeting is at noon' can be a real sentence addressed to someone, so it stays protected (#120 decision, refined by #122 — the test is whether the filler contains a hesitation particle, not whether it has several words)
cases.input: You know the meeting is at noon
cases.expected: You know the meeting is at noon

cases.description: #122 case 1: 'so um' contains the hesitation particle 'um', so it can never open a real sentence and IS relaxed at position 0 — unlike 'you know'. Before #122 the blanket multi-word exclusion left the whole phrase intact
cases.input: So um the meeting is at noon

cases.description: 'so uh' qualifies for the same reason as 'so um'
cases.input: So uh the meeting is at noon

cases.description: #122 boundary decision: 'okay so' has NO hesitation particle — it is two ordinary words and 'Okay so what do you think?' is a legitimate message, so it stays protected
cases.input: Okay so the meeting is at noon
cases.expected: Okay so the meeting is at noon

cases.description: #122 case 2: Whisper writes a hesitation as 'Uh...'; the trailing dot is sentence punctuation, not the dot in 'main.py', so the code-token guard must not fire on it. The filler and its own trailing punctuation both go
the trailing-dot relaxation must not reach 'Actually.' — it is not a hesitation particle, so it stays protected (#122)
sentence-initial 'Right' is content (a direction), not a filler — #120 narrows the #117 relaxation
sentence-initial 'Like' can name a UI element and must not be treated as a filler
sentence-initial 'Actually' can be a real content word
the leading 'Literally' survives while the trailing lowercase 'literally' is still removed as a filler
'err' is an ordinary English verb, so it is not a default filler — this returned 'To is human' until #125. Mid-utterance and lowercase, so no position-0 or capitalisation guard applies
'Err on the side of caution' is an instruction, not a hesitation — 'err' is excluded from the hesitation particles too (#125)
cases.input: Err on the side of caution
cases.expected: Err on the side of caution

cases.description: 'ah' stays a filler where 'err' does not: it is an interjection in every dictionary sense, so removing it costs tone, never meaning (#125 decision)
Rule A must not strip a capitalised token that happens to be a filler word mid-utterance — 'Like' could be a product name
mid-utterance capitalised filler lookalikes stay protected even after the sentence-initial relaxation (#117 option 2)
a filler appearing INSIDE a code identifier must not be stripped — this returned 'call _fn in main.py' until the guard was fixed to test the enclosing token
word boundaries: 'like' inside 'likely' must survive — this returned 'that is ly correct' until a trailing \b was added
a burst containing nothing but fillers
Rule B collapses 2-grams only, so a repeated THREE-word phrase passes through. Pinned so both platforms agree on the limit
cases.input: send it to send it to Alice
cases.expected: send it to send it to Alice

cases.description: Rule B runs to a fixed point, not once
cases.input: go to go to go to line ten

cases.description: 'had had' is grammatical; the filter must not eat real language that merely looks repeated
cases.input: the report that he had had approved
cases.expected: the report that he had had approved

cases.description: Rule C: 'scratch that' rolls back to the last sentence boundary
cases.input: send it to Bob. scratch that send it to Alice
cases.expected: send it to Bob. send it to Alice

cases.description: Rule C: the 'no wait' trigger
cases.input: meet at three. no wait meet at four
cases.expected: meet at three. meet at four

cases.description: Rule C with no preceding sentence to roll back to
cases.input: scratch that send it to Alice

cases.description: the trigger phrase can appear in genuine speech; documents whatever the shipped behaviour is so both platforms agree
cases.input: he said never mind the cost and left

cases.description: ADR-015 collapse is opt-in; a stutter survives by default
ADR-015: hyphenated stutter collapsed when enabled
ADR-015: space-separated stutter fragments
ADR-015: a repeated whole short word
prolongation collapse is opt-in

a run shorter than prolongation_min_run is left alone
text with no disfluency must pass through byte-for-byte
cases.input: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog

cases.input: um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so um so the actual point is here

cases.description: a URL path segment that happens to be a filler word must survive — this ate 'actually' out of the middle of the URL until the guard was fixed
